_comment: Baseline numbers for bin/bench.sh.  Each scenario gets two floors
(mars_parse_MBps and mars_live_MBps) plus a vs-best-other ratio.
If a current measurement falls below the floor, the gate fails.
Tolerances bake observed run-to-run noise (~5-8% headless, ~10% live)
into the floor so the gate doesn't flap on identical code.
Re-baseline: run `bin/bench.sh --update-baseline` after a change
you actually want to lock in.  Re-run cross-terminal numbers via
`bin/measure-other.sh` (now 3-trial median per E5) if the iTerm2 /
Warp comparison drifts.
F gate-lock 2026-05-05 (perf-attack F): clean-machine numbers from
bench-run + measure-other (3-trial), × 0.93 (parse) / 0.90 (live,
ratios) safety margin.  Earlier same-day floors were over-loose due
to godot CPU contention skewing measurements ~30% slower than truth.
These are the *minimum* marspot must hold while A/B/C/D attack work is
ongoing; the targets to break above are tracked outside this repository.
2026-11-22: mcli and the single-process marspot app were deleted.
Binary sizes are judged against bench/size-budget.json (since
2026-11-26).  memory_idle_kb_max is gone: it launched those two
deleted binaries and sampled their RSS, and the shipped equivalent - the
footprint of shell, core and sessions in a window - is not something the
fast gate starts, and no footprint ceiling for the shipped processes
exists yet.  mars_live_MBps_min ('app MB/s', not gating) has read
the shipped app (bin/drivers/marspot.sh run-app) since 2026-11-13, but
its floors 94 / 92 / 92 / 84 were set while live meant mcli.  Re-set to
the lowest reading of the nine `bench.sh --full` runs on mini on
2026-11-15 whose gate passed (of eleven that day;
bench/results/history/app-MB-s-*.jsonl on mini:
ascii 285.1, mixed 254.3, cjk 274.4, emoji 273.2 MB/s, load1 at most
_units: Throughput floors (*_MBps_min) are 10^6 bytes per second.  Until 2026-11-12 the headless parse floors were in 2^20 bytes per second under the same name; they were multiplied by 1.048576 that day, which keeps each floor where it was.  The competitor snapshot states its unit per terminal, see its _unit_note.  *_insn_per_byte_max are instructions retired per byte (lower is better), as the kernel reports them for the measured process: marspot-session for the mars_l3 keys, the whole `marspot --bench parse` process for the mars_parse keys.

scenarios._l3_note: mars_l3_MBps_min: the SHIPPED path (core -> L3, file-backed scrollback), measured by bin/measure-l3.sh and gated by --full since 2026-08-19.  The probe reports the MINIMUM of its trials, not the median: load can only add time, so the fastest trial is the least-contaminated one.  That change is what made this metric usable on a host with a permanent tenant - one batch read 28.7 / 72.3 / 160.0 MiB/s for the same scenario, where a median reports the tenant and the minimum reports marspot.  Floors are min-of-3 x0.90 taken at load1 4.5: 132.8 / 151.0 / 152.9 / 111.9.  Idle best for reference: 194.5 / 167.8 / 172.1 / 125.4 - three of the four are within noise of the loaded reading, which is the point.  ascii is the exception (147.5 loaded vs 194.5 idle): its trial pushes 134 MB and is the likeliest to catch interference in all three tries.  2026-10-17: mixed relocked to 134.2.  Until then an L3 drained its whole PTY queue before going back to its loop, so the probe's 122x39 resize waited for the end of the cat and most trials ran at the startup 80 columns - a narrower grid and less work per line.  The witness shows it (scrollback.bin 48101192 at 80 columns, 48089054 at 122) and so did the instruction count, which split 160 / 196 per byte between trials of one binary.  The old floors were taken from those 80-column trials.  With the pump bounded the resize lands within 8 ms and every trial runs at the width it asked for; three runs at load1 1.6-2.6 read mixed 154.3 / 149.1 / 150.8, and 149.1 x0.90 is the new floor.  The same binary at 122 columns before the change cost 196 instructions a byte against 160 now.  ascii / cjk / emoji still clear their old floors and were left alone; emoji read 108.2 in one of the three runs with all five trials at exactly 1.24 s, cause not found, 126.6 and 134.2 in the others.
scenarios._live_note: mars_vs_best_other_min compares the SHIPPED path (L3) against the best other terminal measured, and is set to 1.0 flat: the requirement is that the product is faster, and a requirement does not get a tolerance band.  That makes this the one floor in the file that can go red from load alone - it divides a number that swings with the host (L3 ascii read 194.5 idle and 134.2 at load1 5.3) by a competitor figure frozen in the snapshot.  Treat a failure here the way bin/bench-remote.sh's load gate says to: valid when idle, re-measure otherwise.  The job of catching a real regression belongs to mars_l3_MBps_min, which carries the margin.  Idle headroom as of 2026-08-19: ascii 1.91x, mixed 1.65x, cjk 1.14x, emoji 1.06x - emoji is the thin one and the next thing worth widening.
scenarios._parse_file_note: mars_parse_file_MBps_min: the SAME headless parse with the scrollback a real pane has. `--bench parse` builds a Terminal with no MARSPOT_SESSION_ID and gets the in-RAM scrollback; every L3 pane sets it and gets the file-backed one, which trims, encodes and writes every scrolled line and keeps a RAM ring besides. Measured on mini 2026-09-07, median of 5: RAM 371.7 / 240.7 / 263.8 / 174.1 against file-backed 126.8 / 121.3 / 122.4 / 113.2 - the write dominates so completely that it flattens four very different corpora into 113-127. The fast gate had only ever shown the RAM number, so a whole afternoon of comparing against Alacritty was done against a path no user runs. (mars_l3_MBps_min covers the shipped path end to end but only under --full; this one isolates parse+scrollback without the L3 IPC.) Floors are min-of-5 x0.95 - this metric's spread is wide (ascii 119.6-155.6 in one batch) and its job is catching a regression, not holding a line.
scenarios._insn_note: Instruction ceilings, set 2026-11-12 from runs of one build (a63c4c4, rustc 1.99.1, mini, under the bench lock, load1 at most 3.2 during the single-session trials).  Each is the worst reading plus a margin sized to that metric's own run-to-run range, (max-min)/median.  mars_l3_insn_per_byte_max: median of 7 trials per run; eight runs read 143.99-146.36 / 178.35-181.83 / 171.76-172.38 / 212.61-215.17 for ascii / mixed / cjk / emoji (range 1.6 / 1.9 / 0.4 / 1.2 %), and two more runs of the same binary earlier the same night read 144.10-147.50 / 182.06-182.40 / 172.67-172.82 / 215.47-215.76.  Ceiling = the worst of the ten x 1.02.  A change that adds 5 % lifts even the lowest of the ten above its ceiling (ascii 143.99 x 1.05 = 151.19 against 150.45, the thinnest of the four).  All ten were taken the way bin/bench-remote.sh runs the probe, over an ssh session that stays open: with the session that started it already closed the same binary reads 4-6 % lower (mixed 170-171), for a reason not yet known, and bin/measure-l3.sh refuses to measure in that state.  mars_parse_insn_per_byte_max: median of 5, eight runs within 0.07 %, ceiling = worst x 1.01.  mars_parse_file_insn_per_byte_max: median of 5, eight runs within 1.0 %, ceiling = worst x 1.02; both are the same to the second decimal however the run is started.  mars_l3_insn_per_byte_max was lowered twice on 2026-11-12, each time to the worst of four runs x 1.02: after scrolled lines were filed as runs and the pty was read in chunks, and after the reader moved to a kqueue (four runs read 95.53-98.14 / 144.07-144.21 / 150.03-150.13 / 191.84-192.32; the trials inside a run sit at two or three levels about 4 apart on mixed and cjk, and the median has not moved between them).  All three instruction rows were lowered again the same day, after a scrolled row was blanked only as far as it was written and bulk output was handed over in full chunks: four runs read 94.57-95.46 / 133.41-133.71 / 141.09-141.51 / 184.66-184.84 for the session, 45.80 / 83.92-83.93 / 90.32-90.33 / 139.83-139.84 / 440.41-440.44 for the parse in memory and 75.83-75.91 / 125.77-125.96 / 139.14-139.25 / 186.88-187.29 for the parse into a file, each ceiling the worst x its margin -- except the session's mixed, cjk and emoji rows.  Their trials sit at two or three levels (mixed 129 / 133.5 / 138, cjk 136.7 / 141 / 146, emoji 184.7 / 187.7) and a fifth run put the emoji median on the upper one (187.67), so those three ceilings are the highest trial of the five runs x 1.02 (138.17, 146.07, 187.82).  All three instruction rows were lowered again on 2026-11-12 (evening), after three changes to the parse thread: text that needs no segmenter (printable ASCII, the wide fast class, emoji-presentation pictographs, in any mix) is written to the row in one pass, the parameters of a control sequence are taken from the read as a slice, and a row that scrolls off is blanked with one copy of a blank row.  Four runs of one build (fdb7b91, mini, under the bench lock, load1 2.8-3.2) read 36.06 / 55.28-55.29 / 59.74-59.75 / 59.14-59.15 / 413.28-413.30 for the parse in memory, 67.12-67.27 / 98.98-99.20 / 110.06-110.34 / 107.61-107.89 for the parse into a file, and, with two more runs of the same binary, 85.11-86.49 / 106.80-108.55 / 112.20-112.86 / 107.85-109.55 for the session (median of 7 trials; range of the six medians 1.6 / 1.6 / 0.6 / 1.6 %).  Each ceiling is the worst reading x its margin (1.01 / 1.02 / 1.02).  The trials inside a session run no longer sit at separate levels: they spread evenly over 83.9-90.3 / 106.4-110.4 / 110.5-115.7 / 107.1-114.3, so the session rows use the same rule as the others and not the highest-trial exception.  What these rows cannot see is time spent storing and copying cells: padding the cell from 20 to 40 bytes raised the instructions of the file-backed parse by 9-15 % and its wall clock by 28-46 %.  The session rows and the file-backed parse rows were lowered again on 2026-11-12 (night), after five changes.  One is to the probe and not to the product: it now starts the session at 122 by 39, where it used to send that size once it could connect and every trial reflowed a few milliseconds of history at 80 columns, so readings from before that day are not of the same thing.  The others: a flood is published one frame per display frame, the newest history lines are kept in memory as the records the file gets, scrolled lines go to their writer threads in buffers eight times the size, and a pane flooding alone asks its pty again after a short read.  Four runs of one build (560c2dc and 0050a35, which differ by a test; mini, under the bench lock, load1 2.1-3.9) read 65.89-65.99 / 88.24-88.32 / 93.37-93.49 / 89.88-89.95 for the session (median of 7 trials) and 57.39-57.41 / 87.03-87.08 / 97.35-97.41 / 95.16-95.28 for the parse into a file; each ceiling is the worst reading x 1.02.  The parse in memory read 36.06-36.07 / 55.29-55.30 / 59.74-59.75 / 59.14-59.15 / 413.27-413.31, where it was, and its ceilings were left alone.  They were set once more on 2026-11-13: the write buffers went back from 512 KiB to 64 KiB, because a pane may not hold more memory than it did, and a writer thread now waits two milliseconds for more buffers and writes them in one call.  Four runs of one build (6dd96f0; mini, under the bench lock, load1 1.5-3.4) read 65.32-65.45 / 87.79-87.97 / 94.12-94.25 / 90.69-90.81 for the session, 94.20-94.47 for nine of them, and 57.97-58.02 / 88.13-88.22 / 102.48-102.58 / 99.67-99.71 for the parse into a file, which hands over eight times as many buffers as it did; each ceiling is the worst reading x 1.02, x 1.05 for the nine.

scenarios._note: Relocked 2026-08-18 after the emoji fast-path attack: floor = 135.  Two mini runs an hour apart gave 153.2 (idle) and 145.0 (load1 4.3); 135 is the loaded run x 0.93, so the gate reports a real regression rather than whoever else happens to be compiling on the bench host.  This REPLACES the 2026-07-11 note, whose reasoning was disproved rather than merely outgrown.  That note read: 'pictographic codepoints cannot take the batch lanes (a following VS16/ZWJ changes width), so they pay the segmenter... the honest ceiling is ~66 MB/s'.  The premise is right and the conclusion does not follow: the fast class already guarantees that a batch commit leaves the LAST character buffered, so a following VS16 / ZWJ / skin-tone modifier still meets an OPEN cluster on the slow path and re-decides its width there.  What genuinely cannot be admitted is a character whose boundary depends on a neighbour - regional indicators (GB12/13) and skin-tone modifiers (GBP=Extend) - and those are two ranges, pinned against the tables by `the_fast_pictograph_class_never_outruns_the_tables` over the whole codepoint space.  Measured 61 -> 153.2 MB/s = 2.15x, with ascii / mixed / cjk unchanged or better.  Full decomposition and the per-change prices are in the perf notes.  mars_live_MBps_min for this scenario was re-set on 2026-11-22 from the shipped app's readings (see the top-level _comment).

scenarios._note: Added 2026-11-14.  Three attributed runs a line and no cell at the default: what coloured output costs, which cat-mixed (six coloured cells a line) does not say.  L3 ceiling = the worst of three interleaved mini rounds (68.27 / 68.29 / 68.31) x 1.02.

Added 2026-11-14.  Twelve colour changes a line with a few characters between them, the shape a syntax highlighter or git diff writes: the cost is entering and leaving text.  L3 ceiling = the worst of three interleaved mini rounds (97.24 / 97.25 / 97.25) x 1.02.

Added 2026-09-30.  cat-emoji is single-codepoint emoji throughout - measured, 4 893 420 clusters and not one over a codepoint - so nothing in this suite exercised the path a real cluster takes, which is the slow one by construction (a regional-indicator pair and a skin-tone modifier are the two things the fast pictograph class cannot admit).  This stream is 36.1% multi-codepoint clusters, widest seven.  Floor 35 = the LOWEST of four mini runs x 0.93, the same rule as cat-emoji's.  38 was set first, from a single 40.9 reading, and straddled the noise: four runs at mini load 6.5-8.3 gave 40.9 / 39.8 / 37.9 / 37.3, so the gate failed twice on the same code.  A floor that fires on whoever else is compiling teaches you to relock rather than to look, which is the failure this whole file argues against.  35 still catches the regression this scenario was written to catch: capturing a scrolled-off cluster by COPYING it rather than moving it read 26.1.  Deliberately pathological: real pane output measured 55 multi-codepoint clusters in forty million, so this number is about a code path and not about a workload.  It is ~10% below where the same stream parsed before the cluster pool existed (47.9 -> 42.8 MB/s on the dev box, three runs each), which is what holding a cluster whole costs when a third of the stream is clusters.

render_full_repaint._comment: p99 across 1000 iterations × median of 3 trials.  Real-world swing on a hot mac is up to ~2 ms (observed range 1.0-1.4 ms across one day's bench runs — 30 % spread driven by GPU thermal + scheduler noise).  Ceiling at 1.8 ms catches an actual regression (1.5x current median) while tolerating that noise.  --update-baseline applies the default 1.10 margin which collapses to the noise floor; manually widened.

scroll_repaint._comment: p99 ns/repaint while walking view_offset from 5000 -> 0 in 3-line steps over 100K-line scroll-history.bin (--bench scroll).  Picks up MARS_DISK_SCROLLBACK so the gate tracks whichever variant is current default.  Median of 5 trials.  Relocked 2026-07-11: 10-sample idle-mini distribution is 3000-3125ns, median 3083ns, stdev ~1% (timer quantum ~41ns) - the old floor 3 was set as 2x a ~1.5us median and never re-widened; same-binary historical readings spanned 1.8-3.1us so no regression vs Jun-6 is provable from available data.  Floor = 3.083 x 1.3 (the 30% margin scroll convention, matching scroll_cold) = 4.  A real >30% scroll regression still fails the gate.

scroll_cold_repaint._comment: Sister gate to scroll_repaint, forced to disk-backed (MARS_DISK_SCROLLBACK=1) and with pages evicted via madvise(DONTNEED) before the walk.  Catches disk-path regressions that the default-env scroll bench misses when memory is the default.  Cold-cache p99 measured ~3-5 µs; same 30 % run-to-run noise as the warm gate, manually widened to ~2x current median.

key_to_frame._comment: 2026-11-22: microseconds from a key event's timestamp to the shell's present call returning, one pane in a 1000x760 pt window, 200 keys a run (runs of 20 `x` then 20 backspaces, 120-150 ms apart), bin/measure-latency.sh scene type-1 inside `bin/bench.sh --full`; the figure is the median over runs 2-4 of each run's percentile (p99 of 200 keys is the third-largest, so the one slow key every run has, 16-27 ms max, does not reach it).  Shell and core are a latency-trace build, the session the shipped binary.  Mini, M4 Pro, macOS 27.2.1, load1 1.3-3.6, commit 7b2701b plus this gate: test-e2e-remote run, 5 rounds: p50 2862 / 2972 / 2944 / 2964 / 2889, p99 3586 / 3863 / 3675 / 3932 / 3882; bench-remote --full run 20261121T220401Z, runs 1-4: p50 2904 / 2977 / 2924 / 2861, p99 3844 / 3709 / 3957 / 3804.  Ceilings = worst reading x margin: p99 3957 x 1.30 = 5144 -> 5150, p50 2977 x 1.20 = 3572 -> 3575 (the p50 spreads 4 % across nine runs, the p99 10 %).  Both gate: the p50 shows a shift every key pays, which a per-run p99 of 200 keys reads through more noise.  Where the p50 goes (2026-11-22, run r1 above): about 1.2 ms of it is the core finding the GPU done, of which 0.15 ms is GPU work and the rest its 1 ms poll; 0.57 ms build + encode + commit; 0.4-0.7 ms the session's round trip; 0.19 ms the shell's present.  A key whose frame was presented after the next key was pressed (over 120 ms) is left out of the percentiles by bin/_latency_report.py, so the gate counts such keys in a row of its own with a ceiling of 0; a run that stopped part way, fewer reports than runs, or a key never followed to a present make every key-to-frame row invalid rather than read from what is left.

competitors_snapshot._comment: Per-terminal version + captured_at. Each entry self-describes when and against what version it was measured, so a snapshot that drifts (one terminal refreshed today, another stuck at an older date) is auditable. `host` describes the bench host all measurements were taken on. bench.sh `vs-best-other` iterates entries with *_MBps keys; `host` / `_comment` are skipped automatically (no key match). terminal.app excluded from the denominator by design (OS-vendor reference floor, not a competitor).  2026-08-18: ghostty + marspot re-measured under a NEW protocol and are NOT comparable with the 2026-06-07 rows above them.  Two changes: (1) every terminal now pushes LIVE_MIN_BYTES (32 MiB) by cat'ing the scenario file as many times as needed — a single 8 MiB pass never blocks `cat` long enough to measure a fast terminal, and the old rows mix per-scenario byte counts; (2) each trial ends with a DSR round-trip (`CSI 6 n`), so the number covers work the terminal has CONFIRMED it consumed.  Without (2) a terminal that drops or coalesces under pressure finishes early and wins — the reason marspot grew DSR support the same day (L2 0.12.138).  iterm/warp/terminal cannot be driven from an ssh session (AppleEvent -1712 under both plain ssh and launchctl asuser for iTerm); they need a console run of bin/measure-other.sh and are stale until then.

iterm2.method: ssh, run inside the GUI session

ghostty.method: ssh, run inside the GUI session

competitors_snapshot._captured_at_note: 2026-08-19: ghostty / iterm2 / terminal / marspot were all measured in ONE run, on one host, under the certified protocol (32 MiB per trial, DSR round-trip) - the first time every terminal in this table was compared under identical conditions rather than assembled from separate sessions.  The absolute numbers are lower than an idle host produces (the run happened at load1 ~6), which is fine and is the point: they are all lower together, so the RATIOS hold.  warp is still 2026-06-07: it has no AppleScript dictionary, so driving it needs System Events keystrokes, which TCC does not grant an ssh session - the reachability probe correctly skipped it instead of inventing a number.  Its old figures sit far below ghostty on every corpus, so it does not affect which terminal is 'best other'.  This note describes the 2026-08-19 capture; every row was re-measured on 2026-11-22 (see _note_20261122), the marspot row then from the shipped three-process app.  The gate's 'app MB/s' rows measure the product on each run and divide by the other terminals' rows; it never reads the marspot row.
competitors_snapshot._unit_note: A terminal's row says which megabyte its numbers are in: "unit": "MB/s" is 10^6 bytes per second, and a row without the key was captured before 2026-11-12 in 2^20 bytes per second.  The gate converts the second kind before comparing.

_comment: Floors for the bench-run.sh scenarios (cat-mixed.9x = multi-session-9x,
scrollback-1m).  Read from bench/results/cross-terminal.json (latest
bench-run.sh snapshot).  Two checks per scenario: marspot's own absolute
throughput floor, and the marspot-vs-best-other ratio floor.  The ratio
floor is the structural protection — without it, marspot and competitors
can both slow down and the gate stays green even though our relative
advantage shrunk.
Locked 2026-05-05 against c43d26b (clean-machine, post-godot-cleanup):
multi-session-9x: marspot 104.6 / iterm 18.2 / terminal 60.1 MiB/s
scrollback-1m:    marspot 97.7  / iterm 71.8 / terminal 91.6 MiB/s
10% safety margin.  Re-lock via `bin/bench.sh --full --update-baseline`
after re-running `bin/bench-run.sh` ≥3× to populate snapshots.
multi_session_thresholds._retired: No longer read by the gate (2026-11-12): nothing the gate runs produced the snapshot these floors are judged against, so the check failed on every run.  Values are 2^20 bytes per second, as locked on 2026-05-05.  multi_session_l3 replaces it.

competitors_snapshot_studio._comment: TAKEN ON THE WRONG HOST, kept as a record rather than deleted. This measurement pushes 32 MB into each terminal and saturates the machine it runs on; run on the studio 2026-09-07 with nine live panes it both disturbed the user's work and contaminated itself - marspot's cat-ascii trials came back 380 / 1710 / 1890 ms and the median took a disturbed one, so the 0.21x below is interference, not a result (the best trial works out to ~88 MB/s, about parity with iTerm2). The other three scenarios were stable to within 10 % and are worth something: marspot 1.77x / 1.88x / 1.74x over the best other on mixed / cjk / emoji. bin/measure-other.sh now refuses to run off the bench host for exactly this reason. bench.sh's vs-best-other reads the mini snapshot, not this one - a ratio only means anything between numbers from the same host at the same time. mini's rows are still from 2026-08-19 and need a Screen-Sharing session there (ssh cannot dispatch AppleEvents); bin/remote-measure-others.sh prints the steps, and the driving is automatic now, so it is one command rather than four pastes.
competitors_snapshot_studio.host: studio (dev box, 9 live panes) - NOT the mini bench host

multi_session_l3._comment: Nine marspot-session processes absorbing the same scenario at once, run by the gate itself (bin/measure-l3.sh --sessions 9).  insn_per_byte_max judges the LOWEST of the trials: instructions summed over the nine sessions, divided by the bytes they absorbed together.  One session alone costs about 181 per byte on this scenario; nine at once cost 193-368 from trial to trial, depending on how much they get in each other's way, and that difference is what this row shows.  Nine runs of one build read a minimum of 192.61-227.85 (range 17 %; the trials inside one run span far more), ceiling = worst x 1.05.  It therefore cannot see a change smaller than about a quarter; the single-session rows are the ones that see 5 %.  The aggregate wall-clock rate (112-130 MB/s best trial in the same runs) is reported and does not gate.  Since readers in bulk output take turns, two at a time (2026-11-12), four runs of one build read 209.50-210.45 and carried 220-223 MB/s together; ceiling = worst x 1.05.  Without the turns the same reader costs 234 a byte here, so this row sees them go missing.  With bulk output handed over in full chunks, four runs read 137.02-137.28 and 263-266 MB/s; ceiling = worst x 1.05.  With text written to the row in one pass and a scrolled row blanked by one copy (2026-11-12, evening), four runs read 108.14-108.43 and 276-278 MB/s; ceiling = worst x 1.05.  With the frame gate, the ring of records, the larger hand-overs to the writer threads and the probe starting its sessions at the pane's size (2026-11-12, night), four runs read 94.42-94.55 and 297-302 MB/s; ceiling = worst x 1.05.

app_footprint_12_panes._comment: Summed phys_footprint of marspot-shell + marspot-core + all 12 marspot-session processes, one window of 4 x 3 panes, each pane printing 40 lines and sitting at a /bin/sh prompt, read once all 12 pane shells run, a frame is on screen and the processes together use under 0.02 of a core over 2 s (bin/measure-app-footprint.sh, run by bin/bench.sh --full inside the console session).  The gate judges the median of the rounds in KiB.  Ceiling from mini 2026-11-22, two runs, 8 rounds: 88710368 to 89152688 bytes (about 84.6 to 85.0 MiB: shell 22.6-22.9, core 38.1-38.3, sessions 1.95-2.05 MiB each, 23.8-24.1 together).  Worst 89152688 B = 87063 KiB, x 1.05 = 91417 KiB.  The rounds agree within 0.5 %, so 5 % is about 4.3 MiB: a session growing by a third of a MiB, or the shell or core by a tenth of itself, trips it.

app_startup._comment: Milliseconds from exec of marspot-shell (sandbox, the shipped three processes, one window of one pane) to the core's WINDOW_FIRST_CONTENT: the shell reported shown the first frame in which the pane shows what its shell printed (bin/measure-startup.sh, run by bin/bench.sh --full in the console session).  cold = first launch of copies signed again ad hoc under a fresh identifier (new inode, new code hash); warm = the same copies launched again right after; the gate judges the median of the trials.  Mini 2026-11-22, two runs: cold 250 163 180 168 163 (median 168, load1 about 2) and 181 156 175 164 160 176 178 (median 175, load1 4-7); warm 144 157 163 147 168 (157) and 179 164 158 157 170 163 171 (164).  Of the time, about 65 ms is before the core is spawned and 35-50 ms is the session's boot.  Cold and warm differ by about 10 ms, inside the spread of either: on mini a never-seen code hash costs nothing measurable at first exec, so the cold row does not yet show a first-launch cost of its own.  Both gate: run medians agreed within 5 % with the host at load 2 and at load 7, so a ceiling of the worst median x 1.5 (cold 175 -> 263, warm 164 -> 246) leaves the host's noise far below the line and still catches a startup that grows by half.

pane_control._comment: P95 in ms of the pane control socket's latencies, each from the request leaving the probe to its answer arriving, on connections kept open and paced under the per-caller rate (bin/measure-pane-control.sh + bin/_pane_control_probe.py, run by bin/bench.sh --full in the console session; one window, a pane reading its input silently and a pane at a /bin/sh prompt).  send: one byte without Enter, answered once written to the PTY.  send_enter: the same with Enter, including the 50 ms the session leaves for the echo.  fired: a `change` wait, from the answer to the send that makes the shell echo to the answer to the wait.  run_true: pane.run true, to the answer with its exit status; runs paced 200 ms apart: input to a pane within 2 s of a run's end there first waits for a prompt watch (shell in front, 150 ms quiet), which a prompt drawn by then answers at once.  run_after_run: the same with each run sent as soon as the one before answered, so it includes that prompt wait.  read: pane.read without history (asks the session nothing, answers no pos).  Mini 2026-11-23, two runs at load1 about 3 (the second after the prompt wait was fixed, so run_true is from it alone): send 0.722 / 1.404, send_enter 60.714 / 61.355, fired 1.25 / 1.677, run_true 164.443, read 1.375 / 2.175.  run_true and read again on mini 2026-11-23 at load1 2.1, one run, after the prompt wait moved to the next input and the plain read stopped asking the session: send 1.27, send_enter 61.401, fired 1.823, run_true 5.257, read 1.611 (a second run waited behind another session's heavy lock on mini and was stopped).  Mini 2026-11-23 after the next input after a run started waiting for the prompt watch instead of a fixed 150 ms, one run at load1 8 (over the reading limit, so the numbers are high if anything): send 1.011, send_enter 60.996, fired 1.575, run_true 5.666, run_after_run 162.624, read 1.131; the earlier ceilings hold, run_after_run gets its first.  Ceiling = the worse run's P95 x 3.  open_shadow: pane.open of a shadow pane to the answer of a `true` run in it, six opens paced 10.5 s apart under the per-parent rate of new panes (6 a minute; ten at once had the probe refused and stop).  Mini 2026-11-23 with PaneControlCaps bit 1 (develop 9be1053 plus the probe pacing), two runs at load1 12.7 and 3.1: send 1.48 / 1.211, send_enter 61.469 / 61.579, fired 1.959 / 1.797, run_true 5.667 / 5.193, run_after_run 162.88 / 162.878, read 1.408 / 1.536, open_shadow 76.952 / 78.644; the earlier ceilings hold, open_shadow gets 3 x 78.644 = 235.9 (the design budget is 500).
